analysis.one_liner: Ends federal income tax on Social Security benefits, paid for with new payroll taxes on income above $250,000.
analysis.headline: Gallego's bill to stop taxing Social Security benefits went to the Senate Finance Committee in September 2025 and has had no hearing, no vote, and zero cosponsors since.
analysis.plain_summary: Today, retirees with income beyond their Social Security check can owe federal income tax on up to 85% of their benefits. This bill would repeal that tax entirely, starting after enactment. To cover the lost money, it would for the first time apply Social Security payroll taxes to wages and self-employment income above $250,000 a year (the tax currently stops at a much lower cap) and would credit a small slice of those high earnings toward a beneficiary's benefit formula. It also backfills the Social Security and Medicare trust funds so they aren't shortchanged by the repeal.
analysis.who_benefits: Retirees and disability beneficiaries who currently pay income tax on part of their benefits would keep more of every check. Higher-income seniors — those most likely to owe the tax — would see the biggest dollar savings, while lower-income beneficiaries who already pay little or nothing would see little change. Poorer seniors on SSI, Medicaid, or CHIP are held harmless so the new benefit formula can't shrink or complicate their other benefits.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the section of the tax code (Section 86) that puts Social Security benefits into taxable income, ending the tax on benefits for every taxable year after enactment.

It appropriates federal money to hold the Social Security and Medicare trust funds (and the Railroad Retirement funds) harmless, replacing the transfers they would lose when the tax on benefits disappears.
It protects SSI, Medicaid, and CHIP beneficiaries by deeming their Social Security benefit no larger than under current law, so the new rules can't disrupt their eligibility or benefit amounts.

analysis.who_pays: Workers and employers would pay Social Security payroll tax on wages above $250,000 a year starting in 2026, and self-employed people would pay on earnings above $250,000 — income that is currently exempt above a much lower annual cap. High earners would get only a partial offset: a 2% benefit factor on earnings above $250,000, applied only to people not yet receiving benefits. General taxpayers bear the cost of the appropriation that backfills the trust funds.

drawbacks.text: The payroll tax increase on top earners is far larger than their added benefits: they would owe the full combined Social Security tax on income above $250,000 but earn credit for only a 2% benefit factor on that earnings, so for people not yet retired this works substantially as a net tax increase on high earners.

Repealing the tax on benefits helps higher-income seniors the most, since lower-income beneficiaries already owe little or no tax on their benefits — critics can fairly call this a tax cut skewed toward affluent retirees.

The bill replaces the trust funds' lost revenue with a general-Treasury appropriation rather than a fully matched pay-for, and no official cost estimate appears in the provided record, so the net effect on the deficit is not established here.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real and plainly stated in the bill text: seniors stop paying income tax on benefits, and high earners start paying payroll tax above $250,000. The main design weakness is the lopsided benefit formula for high earners — they pay the full tax but earn only a sliver of extra benefit — which makes the top end of the payroll tax feel more like a straight tax increase than an earned benefit. The benefit-tax repeal is also regressive across the retiree population, helping the most the retirees who owe the most tax. The trust-fund hold-harmless is a plus, but with no cost estimate in the record the overall fiscal math is unverified.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the Senate, read twice, and referred to the Finance Committee, where it has sat with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Senator Ruben Gallego introduced S. 2716 on September 4, 2025.
The same day, the Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
The bill has zero cosponsors, so no other senator has attached their name to it.
No further action — hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill has not moved, the current rules stay in place for now: high earners keep their payroll-tax exemption above the existing cap, and seniors keep paying income tax on taxable benefits. Neither side has actually won or lost yet.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: High earners, so far — status quo holds

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the Senate Finance Committee; the only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Finance
against.role: Committee of referral, chaired by Sen. Mike Crapo (R-UT)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and has not scheduled a hearing or markup on it; no committee action appears in the record since September 2025.

sides.party_line_note: There has been no vote, and the bill has no cosponsors; it is a Democratic-sponsored tax change whose fate has not yet produced a partisan record.

industries.industry: High-earning households (wages and self-employment income above $250,000)
industries.note: For the first time they would owe Social Security payroll tax on income above $250,000 a year; their interest in keeping the current cap exemption runs directly against retirees' interest in an untaxed benefit. Only a small 2% benefit factor offsets the new tax for future retirees.

These are the retirees whose benefits are currently taxable — up to 85% — so they keep the most from repeal. This is a constituency, not an industry, but it is the group with the largest dollar stake.

analysis.trajectory: Realistically low. A single-sponsor bill with zero cosponsors that has sat in the Finance Committee since September 2025 is unlikely to get a markup, let alone a floor vote, in this Congress; changes to Social Security's tax base have historically required a broader bipartisan negotiation.
